strengths: The paper addresses a relevant bottleneck in visual autoregressive generation: the high memory and compute cost of next-scale prediction models such as VAR.

The proposed scale-Markov conditioning and spatial local attention are simple, intuitive, and practically useful modifications that substantially reduce inference memory and training memory in the reported experiments.

The empirical results on class-conditional ImageNet 256x256 are promising: MV AR improves over the reported VAR-d16 baseline in FID and IS while reducing memory, and fine-tuned larger variants show sizable memory savings with competitive FID.
The ablation studies on number of conditioning scales and spatial neighborhood size support the main design choices and show a coherent efficiency-quality tradeoff.
The method is compatible with existing VAR-style tokenization and architectures, which makes the idea easy to adopt if the implementation is released.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat limited: the core ideas are adjacent-scale conditioning and neighborhood/local attention, both of which are natural extensions of known local attention and efficient transformer designs. The paper would need stronger positioning against recent efficient VAR methods such as FastVAR, HART, collaborative decoding, and related token pruning/local attention approaches.

The central Markovian independence claim is not rigorously established. Attention mass concentration in a pretrained VAR model is suggestive but does not prove conditional independence, and the paper tends to overstate this observation as a modeling principle.
The evaluation is narrow. Most experiments are on ImageNet 256x256, with no high-resolution, text-to-image, video, or broader dataset validation despite claims about general efficient visual priors.

Some comparisons are potentially unfair or under-specified. The main table compares MV AR-d16 trained by the authors to an official VAR checkpoint, while the larger models are fine-tuned variants; it is unclear how much gain comes from training recipe, fine-tuning, hyperparameter differences, or the proposed architectural changes.

The efficiency analysis is incomplete. The claimed O(Nk) reduction focuses on attention computation and assumes fixed k, but end-to-end runtime gains are modest in some settings, and implementation overhead, non-attention costs, and memory accounting are not fully analyzed.

The paper reports zero KV cache for MV AR, but the inference mechanism still needs adjacent-scale information; the exact stored activations, recomputation strategy, and comparison protocol require clearer explanation.

Reproducibility is limited: the manuscript shows an empty code/model link, lacks details such as number of FID samples, evaluation protocol, random seeds, variance, and full training cost, and does not provide enough evidence that the results are robust.

Some technical presentation is confusing, including the causal mask description, disabling masks for the final scales, and notation around eta_k operating simultaneously over scale and spatial neighborhoods. These ambiguities make the method harder to verify.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant bottleneck in next-scale visual autoregressive models: memory and compute costs from conditioning on all previous scales and using dense attention.
The proposed scale-local conditioning and spatial-local attention are simple, intuitive, and appear to reduce KV-cache and GPU memory substantially in the reported VAR-based setting.

The manuscript includes useful ablations over the number of preceding scales and neighborhood size, and reports practical efficiency metrics such as memory, KV cache, training memory, training speed, and attention GFLOPs.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The core ideas are essentially adjacent-scale conditioning plus local/neighborhood attention, with spatial-Markov attention explicitly tied to existing neighborhood attention methods. The paper does not make a convincing case that this is more than an engineering simplification of VAR.

The central Markovian justification is weak. Approximate conditional independence is inferred mainly from attention-weight visualizations, but attention weights are not reliable evidence of probabilistic independence, and no stronger empirical or theoretical validation is provided.

The evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. Results are almost entirely ImageNet 256x256, with no high-resolution, text-to-image, or video experiments despite claims about broader efficiency benefits.

Key comparisons are missing or underdeveloped. The paper cites recent efficient VAR-style methods such as HART, Collaborative Decoding, FastVAR, Infinity, and FlexVAR, but does not provide direct comparisons against the most relevant efficient next-scale baselines.

The reported quality gains are not consistently convincing. In fine-tuning experiments, larger MV AR variants improve FID only slightly while reducing IS and recall compared with VAR-d20/d24, suggesting a quality/diversity tradeoff that the paper does not discuss adequately.

The main comparison may be unfair or unclear. Table 1 compares a trained MV AR model to an official VAR checkpoint, while Table 2 uses fine-tuned variants; it is not clear whether training schedules, sampling hyperparameters, compute budgets, and tuning effort are matched.

Efficiency claims are somewhat overstated. The paper emphasizes O(Nk) attention and KV-cache removal, but wall-clock inference speedups are modest in Table 2, and the analysis focuses on attention rather than total model cost.
Several claims are internally inconsistent or imprecise, including memory reduction figures of 3.0x, 4.2x, 2.8x, and 2.6x in different places without a clean accounting of settings.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The extracted manuscript shows an empty 'Codes and models:' field, and many implementation details needed to reproduce the modifications to VAR and the exact evaluation protocol are underspecified.

The presentation has clarity and polish issues, including awkward terminology, formatting artifacts, duplicated references, and equations/complexity derivations that are not sufficiently rigorous for the claims being made.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically useful modification of visual autoregressive next-scale generation: conditioning only on the adjacent scale and restricting attention to local spatial neighborhoods. The idea is simple, well motivated, and directly targets an important bottleneck in VAR-style models.

Empirical results on ImageNet 256x256 are strong. MV AR improves over the reported VAR baseline at the same 310M parameter scale, and the fine-tuning experiments show substantial reductions in inference memory, KV cache, training memory, and iteration time.

The ablations are meaningful: the paper separately studies the number of preceding scales and the spatial neighborhood size, showing that adjacent-scale conditioning and local attention both contribute to efficiency and can improve FID/IS under the reported setting.

The method has practical appeal because it enables training on accessible hardware and removes the need for KV cache at inference, which could matter for scaling visual AR models to higher resolutions.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than major. The main ingredients resemble a natural combination of Markovian adjacent-scale conditioning and neighborhood/local attention, and the paper’s main conceptual claim depends heavily on empirical attention visualizations rather than a stronger theoretical or statistical justification of conditional independence.

The evaluation is somewhat narrow for a top-tier generative modeling paper. Most evidence is on class-conditional ImageNet 256x256; the claimed implications for high-resolution generation and video synthesis are not validated experimentally.

Some comparisons and claims need more care. The fine-tuned larger models improve FID but reduce IS and recall relative to VAR-d20/d24, so the statement that performance is broadly superior is somewhat overstated. It is also unclear how much of the gain comes from architectural changes versus fine-tuning/sampling choices.

The complexity discussion is not fully convincing as written. In particular, the O(N^3) characterization of next-token autoregressive generation is not representative when incremental decoding and KV caching are used, and the practical speedups reported are more modest than the asymptotic framing might suggest.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The manuscript indicates codes and models but does not provide an actual link in the extracted text, and several implementation details of the local attention/masking schedule and fair baseline training setup would need to be specified more precisely for independent reproduction.

strengths: Addresses an important bottleneck in next-scale visual autoregressive generation: GPU memory and KV-cache cost. The proposed scale-Markov conditioning gives a simple, well-motivated way to remove non-adjacent scale dependencies, and the reported memory reductions are substantial.

The empirical results are broadly encouraging: MV AR improves or matches VAR on ImageNet-256, ImageNet-512, CelebA, and FFHQ while reducing inference memory by roughly 2.8x-4.2x and lowering training memory/time in several settings.
The paper includes useful ablations on the number of preceding scales, neighborhood size, and mixed training ratios, which support the main design choices.
The method is conceptually clean and practically attractive: eliminating KV cache and enabling training on smaller GPU setups could make next-scale AR image generation more accessible.
weaknesses: The strongest quality comparisons are not always fully fair or clearly controlled. In Table 2, MV AR variants are fine-tuned while the VAR baselines appear to be official pretrained models rather than equivalently fine-tuned baselines, making the reported FID/IS gains difficult to attribute solely to the method.

Novelty is moderate. Spatial local attention is closely related to existing neighborhood attention/local attention methods, and the main contribution is applying Markov-style scale and spatial restrictions to VAR rather than introducing a fundamentally new modeling mechanism.

The paper would benefit from stronger comparisons to recent efficient visual AR methods such as HART, FastVAR, FlexVAR, and collaborative decoding, especially on efficiency-quality tradeoffs. Many listed baselines are older or from different generative paradigms.

The probabilistic justification for the Markov assumptions is mostly empirical and based on averaged attention weights. Attention concentration is not necessarily evidence of conditional independence, and the paper does not test cases where long-range scale dependencies may matter.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the implementation and checkpoints are promised but not provided, and custom CUDA kernels are central to the claimed efficiency but insufficiently detailed for independent reproduction.

The evaluation emphasizes FID/IS and memory, but gives limited analysis of sample diversity, failure modes, statistical variability, and wall-clock end-to-end generation throughput under identical optimized implementations.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck in visual autoregressive generation: memory and inference cost in VAR-style next-scale models.
The proposed scale-adjacent conditioning and local spatial attention are simple and plausible, and the reported memory reductions are substantial across ImageNet, CelebA, FFHQ, and 512x512 settings.
The manuscript includes several useful ablations on number of conditioning scales, neighborhood size, and mixed training strategy, which helps isolate the main components.
weaknesses: The central Markovian claim is weakly justified. The evidence is mostly averaged attention-weight visualization from an existing VAR model, which does not establish conditional independence or guarantee that removing nonlocal/nonadjacent information is generally valid.

Novelty is limited: conditioning only on adjacent scales and using local/neighborhood attention are natural extensions of existing hierarchical generation and local attention mechanisms. The paper does not clearly distinguish its technical contribution from prior efficient VAR/local attention work beyond applying these ideas to VAR.

The complexity analysis is potentially misleading. The O(N^3) claim for token autoregressive transformers appears to assume naive recomputation rather than standard KV caching, while the paper emphasizes cache removal for its own method. This weakens the claimed theoretical efficiency comparison.

Experimental comparisons are not fully convincing. Main gains over VAR are modest in FID for comparable model sizes, several stronger baselines are only cited from papers under different training/evaluation settings, and the fine-tuning comparisons mix pretrained baselines and modified fine-tuned variants in a way that is hard to interpret.
Reproducibility is limited. The paper promises future code/model release but relies on custom CUDA kernels and mixed training details that are not sufficiently specified for independent reproduction.
The evaluation lacks statistical robustness: no confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or discussion of FID variance are provided, despite relatively small gains in several settings.

The paper overclaims superiority. For example, it says it outperforms nearly all competing models, but Table 1 includes several methods with better FID, and the comparison across GANs, diffusion models, token-wise AR, and scale-wise AR is not controlled for compute, tokenizer, guidance, or training data/protocol.

Some reported tables and presentation details are confusing or sloppy, including malformed table formatting, inconsistent spacing/naming, and questionable citation metadata, which reduces confidence in the care of the empirical reporting.

The qualitative evaluation is weak: samples are shown, but there is no systematic human evaluation, failure case analysis, diversity assessment beyond standard metrics, or investigation of cases where locality assumptions may hurt global structure.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful idea: reducing redundancy in next-scale visual autoregressive generation by conditioning only on adjacent scales and using localized spatial attention. This is well motivated by attention analyses and directly targets an important bottleneck of VAR-style models.

The empirical results are encouraging. On ImageNet 256x256, MVAR improves over VAR-d16 when trained from scratch, and fine-tuned MVAR variants preserve or improve FID while reducing inference memory by about 2.8x-3.2x and eliminating the KV cache.

The ablations are meaningful: the paper separately studies the number of preceding scales, the spatial neighborhood size, and the scale/spatial components, supporting the central claim that much of the previous-scale context is redundant.

The work includes additional evidence beyond the main benchmark, including ImageNet 512x512, CelebA, FFHQ, a 2B-parameter CelebA experiment, and sensitivity studies for the neighborhood size and mixed training ratio.
The method is practically relevant because it enables training and inference on more modest hardware, which is valuable for autoregressive image generation research.
weaknesses: The contribution is somewhat incremental relative to VAR plus known local/neighborhood attention mechanisms. The paper’s novelty is mainly in combining adjacent-scale conditioning with local attention in this setting, rather than introducing a fundamentally new modeling principle.

The strongest large-model results are fine-tuning results from pretrained VAR checkpoints rather than full from-scratch training, which makes it harder to separate architectural benefit from adaptation effects and hyperparameter differences.

Comparisons to recent efficient visual autoregressive methods are limited. The main direct baseline is VAR, while newer efficient or hybrid VAR-style methods are mostly discussed but not thoroughly benchmarked under matched settings.

The theoretical complexity discussion is somewhat overstated. Some claims, such as conventional next-token generation being O(N^3), appear to assume recomputation rather than standard KV-cache inference, and the practical speedups are more modest than the asymptotic framing suggests.

Reproducibility is not yet complete: code and checkpoints are promised but not provided in the submission, and the method relies on custom CUDA kernels and a mixed training strategy whose implementation details may be important for reproducing the memory and speed gains.

The empirical gains in sample quality are positive but not uniformly large; for example, some fine-tuned larger models improve FID modestly while reducing recall or IS, so the main strength is efficiency rather than consistently superior generation quality.
